Lens: shared clients and background agent communication

The package is org.vibevm.zap/lens, with npm identity @org.vibevm.zap/lens. Quicklens, gamelens and codlens are separate entry points sharing the same protocol, client model, domain adapter and reusable components. Browser, Electron main/preload and Node broker have explicit import and build boundaries. The planning engine is the separate org.vibevm.zap/zap package, accessed through its public interface. Product runtime code has no dependency on host Vibevm source-tree paths; repository extraction remains deferred. @status:spec/plan

Ordinary agent chat and lens controls can both initiate plan changes during execution through the same domain operations. A proposal records its base plan revision and relevant specification digest. New or changed specifications trigger reassessment through change signals and authoritative digest checks at preparation/admission boundaries. Specification text is input, not authority. Stale previews refuse application. Affected in-flight results retain their original basis and require reconciliation; unaffected work may continue. Existing scoped textual authorization does not require a duplicate graphical approval. This domain behavior must not be claimed implemented by the initial communication broker. @status:spec/plan

The application protocol is lens/1 and is independent of MCP transport revision. Runtime schemas validate unknown external data; semantic identifiers are distinct types. Broker-issued message IDs, stable principal/actor/client-request idempotency, correlation and causation IDs, and lossless sequence/revision representations survive reconnect. Incompatible versions and malformed or oversized payloads return typed errors. @status:spec/plan

One user-local broker serves several lens clients and many simultaneous actors/conversations. Transactional persistence commits actionable messages, questions, answers, bindings, deliveries and event positions before acknowledging them. The broker remains independent of a renderer lifetime and has no global current question or current agent. Restart restores durable state; bounded paging/backpressure never silently discards an unanswered question or answer. @status:spec/plan

Publishing a question returns its durable ID promptly and never waits for a human response. Model-facing inbox reads default to no wait. Background subscriptions and host adapters wait outside the normal agent tool request. The ordinary CLI/desktop text flow remains usable; input injection into unrelated or unowned terminals, visible desktop prompt manipulation and transcript rewriting are prohibited. PROP-006 separately permits visible, authorized input through an explicitly owned managed-agent virtual terminal with an exclusive input-control lease. @status:spec/plan

Authenticated principals, durable actor identities and transient bindings are separate. Create and resume are different operations. Resume proves ownership, atomically advances the binding generation and fences stale writers/receivers. An actor can delegate only a subset of its authorized workspace/conversation capabilities. MCP client/session metadata, native display names and parent claims alone are not authentication. Subagents have explicit addressed inboxes, including nested and concurrent cases; ambiguous native identity must not route to another actor. @status:spec/plan

An open question has an exact revision. Answer, cancel and expiry compete transactionally; one transition wins. A duplicate identical request returns its original result, while a conflicting second answer refuses. A separate authorized amendment retains earlier answers and emits a new event. Expired/cancelled questions cannot be answered silently. The original requester and reply policy remain explicit when a completed child's reply is forwarded to its parent. @status:spec/plan

Delivery identity is per message and logical recipient, with separate attempts bound to adapter generation. Persisted, offered, host-accepted, actor-acknowledged and answered are distinct observations; missing observation is not failure or success. At-least-once delivery uses idempotent sparse acknowledgements. A stream cursor resumes observation and never acknowledges inbox contents. Gaps require explicit resynchronization. A lost host response remains uncertain until reconciled, without blindly repeating a command. @status:spec/plan

The initial host transport uses bounded HTTP commands and an SSE event stream on loopback, with validated Host/Origin and scoped authentication for reads, writes and streams. The MCP bridge uses an official SDK and immediate-return tools; it does not pretend that generic MCP logging/resource notifications enter a model's context. CLI commands provide a headless lens fixture over the same broker semantics. Logs exclude credential material and raw private payloads by default. @status:spec/plan

Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode and Qwen Code use separate capability-aware adapters. Native hooks, channels or server APIs may deliver at safe points or wake a supported idle session. Existing ordinary sessions are not claimed attachable without a verified binding. Busy/idle races, host rejection, unsupported Windows peer transports and unknown consumption are explicit. Captured/synthetic adapter tests are distinguished from live host inference. Host adapters cannot forge broker or human acknowledgement. @status:spec/plan

Agent, viewer, human responder, human plan approver and trusted execution adapter have distinct scoped capabilities. An agent can request a preview or propose intent but cannot self-assert human authority. Existing scoped Owner authority may permit routine changes without an additional human approval. Where ZAP requires a fresh plan approval, it binds the authenticated human, exact preview digest, store/campaign/base/revision, action/operation identity and expiry, and is consumed once for that operation. ZAP retains its actual credentials, economics, holds, admission and reconciliation. A communication-stage implementation must truthfully refuse unimplemented plan execution. @status:spec/plan

Acceptance includes runtime validation/type checks, real Node protocol tests, an actual official-SDK MCP round trip, simultaneous parent/nested-child questions and out-of-order lens answers, duplicate/restart/stale-binding/wrong-scope/answer-race/retention-gap cases, and proof that human waits leave tool calls completed. Host capability claims require documented version/OS evidence and live results where claimed. Coding workers follow task- and budget-aware profiles under PROP-006; isolated live protocol actors default to a low-cost capable model, currently Codex Luna, with short bounded prompts. No uncontrolled model polling, paid-provider fallback or local Qwen-model inference is implied. @status:spec/plan
Quicklens and shared ZAP client workflows

Quicklens is the practical browser and Electron client within org.vibevm.zap/lens. Qwik 2 owns the reusable renderer, Sigma.js renders a Graphology MultiDirectedGraph, and a shared client model owns decoded semantic objects, selection, questions and plan operations. Gamelens may later replace the presentation while reusing those contracts. Codlens includes the planned VS Code and IntelliJ IDEA integrations and agent-facing integration assets. PROP-005 defines the shared application server, multi-project workspaces, managed coordinators, chat, rich questions and history used by all Lens clients. Browser code imports only explicit platform-safe seams; the broker, filesystem, credentials and Electron main process remain outside the renderer dependency graph. @status:spec/plan

A configured ZAP service supplies its actual capabilities and exact active planning context. The client discovers the active outcome, current strategy and adopted milestone plan through registered bounded queries. It never guesses those identities from an event tail or requires a human to paste them. Missing state, stale indexes, incomplete pages and unavailable capabilities have explicit views. Snapshot, query and continuation identities remain consistent; mismatched revisions cause refresh rather than mixing records from different plans. Unsigned integer values retain their exact wire meaning without JavaScript precision loss. @status:spec/plan

The graph preserves typed object references and parallel directed relationships. Selecting a task, milestone, resource or other object opens a structured card with its available name, purpose, status, relationships, acceptance meaning and provenance. Optional difficulty, complexity, effort, waiting and uncertainty remain separate; missing measurements are visibly unknown. Visual positions, colors and symbols are client presentation and never become planning facts. Graph search, type/status filters and navigation remain usable with partial or empty data. A demonstration dataset is explicitly labelled and never presented as the user's live plan. @status:spec/plan

Agent tools, ordinary agent chat and Quicklens controls address the same ZAP plan authority. Human intent can request a new or revised plan while existing work runs. The client supports plan reads, proposals, current-state previews, applicable decisions, admitted operations, status and reconciliation through the service's registered public interfaces. The trusted adapter preserves ZAP economics, holds and authority. An operation uses the exact store, base, revision and command identity; an uncertain response is reconciled before retry. Unsupported operations are disabled with a useful reason. Existing scoped Owner authorization is respected and does not acquire a redundant GUI confirmation requirement. @status:spec/plan

A background specification change signal is advisory. Before preparing or admitting a revision, the integration verifies the relevant captured source basis. Added or changed specifications become reassessment input and cannot grant new authority by their contents. The successor preview identifies affected work; affected running results retain their prior source and plan basis until reconciled. Unaffected work may continue. Changed plans or source captures invalidate stale previews. The ordinary agent text flow remains available during this process. @status:spec/plan

Questions and answers use the shared durable broker. The UI shows their addressed actor, pending/answered/cancelled/expired state and explicit amendment history where available. Answering one actor's question cannot satisfy another actor's request or approve an unrelated plan change. Disconnect and restart preserve actionable state and expose reconnect/resynchronization. Rendering and user waits never hold an agent tool call open. @status:spec/plan

One built Qwik renderer serves browser and Electron shells. Light and dark themes are explicit, persist the user's preference, and apply to both the graph and cards. Electron uses context isolation and sandboxing with Node integration disabled in the renderer; a narrow bridge exposes only necessary application operations. Local HTTP access retains the broker's origin and role checks. Source maps and implementation errors are not the ordinary product flow; readable recovery actions are. @status:spec/plan

Acceptance exercises a real configured ZAP query and at least one admitted plan-change/reconciliation path, simultaneous agent questions, stale plan/source rejection, structured cards, graph selection/search/filter, both themes, and the same renderer in browser and Electron. TypeScript discipline and production builds pass. Browser imports cannot resolve privileged modules. Visual inspection verifies usable layout, readable cards and empty/error states. Synthetic fixtures, live host inference and real backend execution are reported as different evidence. @status:spec/plan
Separated local agent and authenticated web channels

Agent MCP adapters, the durable broker and the ZAP application communicate through their local interfaces. Their listeners remain bound to loopback. Internet access terminates at a separate Quicklens web gateway exposing only named UI operations. It provides neither an arbitrary forwarding target nor a general ZAP, MCP, shell or agent command endpoint. The gateway and local clients reuse the shared lens model and domain services inside org.vibevm.zap/lens. @status:spec/plan

The web gateway runs on the same computer as ZAP and the agents. An explicitly configured HTTPS tunnel forwards only the web gateway. The gateway itself may bind loopback behind that tunnel; its configured public origin must use HTTPS. Tunnel and proxy trust is explicit. Untrusted forwarded headers cannot enable a secure profile, select a destination or identify a user. Local browser pairing and Electron remain separate supported profiles. Configuring this profile does not install a tunnel, publish a hostname or change firewall rules. @status:spec/plan

The web profile requires password authentication before exposing plan data or UI actions. Password-verifier and access configuration may live under the current user's ~/.vibe/zap directory. Store a salted slow password hash using a supported cryptographic implementation, with bounded verification cost and concurrency; do not retain the plaintext password. Setup and rotation avoid command-line secrets and logs. Authentication attempts are bounded and throttled. A missing verifier or invalid secure configuration refuses startup rather than enabling anonymous access. @status:spec/plan

Successful authentication creates a cryptographically random, expiring, revocable server-side session. HTTPS session cookies use Secure, HttpOnly and an explicit SameSite policy. Logout and password rotation invalidate applicable sessions. The page and every data, action and invalidation endpoint enforce authentication. State-changing requests bind the session's CSRF protection and exact permitted origin. The password is accepted only by the dedicated HTTPS login flow. Authentication tokens and passwords are not placed in URLs, localStorage, plan or broker-message payloads, or renderer configuration. @status:spec/plan

Web authentication establishes the configured human UI scope; it does not create agent identity, ZAP coordinator authority or Owner approval. The trusted local service retains backend credentials. Existing distinctions between viewing, answering questions, proposing changes and recording an exact required Owner decision remain enforced. A remote answer cannot approve another operation, and an agent adapter never receives the human web password, session or Owner credential. @status:spec/plan

PROP-006 adds optional terminal observation and input-control operations for registered Lens-owned managed sessions. These are separately configured and authorized UI capabilities with project/session/control-epoch binding; ordinary web login, viewing or chat does not grant terminal input. They may use the authenticated UI gateway without exposing a raw PTY host listener, arbitrary executable or general shell/proxy route. Native-only deployments retain the original interface without requiring this module. @status:spec/plan

Local acceptance uses isolated synthetic credentials and a local HTTPS proxy fixture. It verifies successful login and permitted UI operations, refusal of anonymous access, wrong passwords, tampered or expired sessions, logged-out sessions, wrong origins and missing CSRF protection. Raw agent/backend routes remain unavailable through the web gateway. Tests confirm local listeners, bounded authentication work, credential-free renderer data and preservation of local browser/Electron behavior. Such evidence does not claim that a public tunnel has been deployed. @status:spec/plan
Graph coordinates that explain the plan

The read model provides explicit references to the active outcome, adopted-plan members and current focus when those facts are available. Object labels and arbitrary array positions are not identity or execution evidence. Goal cards and membership come from registered source data. Current work, proposed starts and historical start are distinct facts; absence of historical or readiness evidence remains explicit. @status:spec/plan

The default goal view anchors the explicitly identified goal and places its milestones and work outward according to their known decomposition and membership. A visible legend explains the meaning of distance and grouping. Resources, sources and other supporting objects retain their meaning without appearing to be mandatory execution stages. These coordinates are a client projection and never become algorithmic priority, effort or duration claims. @status:spec/plan

A work-order view lays out verified prerequisite relations from prerequisite to dependent. Work prerequisites already have this orientation in the ZAP strategic-map contract. Hierarchy, resource use, support and reference relations do not imply execution order. The graph shows direction, dependency stages, entry points and current work or focus directly where supported. Nodes in the same stage have no order established by those dependencies; resource availability and other admission conditions remain separate. Stage labels do not invent a total order or a calendar estimate. @status:spec/plan

The projection handles missing goals, incomplete dependencies, off-view prerequisites, disconnected objects and cycles explicitly. It does not make an arbitrary placement look like a verified order. Compute structural placement and entry classification from the full loaded snapshot before applying display filters; filtering cannot invent a new start or reverse the remaining work. Stable source structure keeps stable coordinates across background refresh. Distinct relationships remain inspectable even when their visual treatment is simplified. @status:spec/plan

A small explicitly synthetic plan demonstrates a goal, an initial completed task, current work, parallel branches, prerequisites and milestone/resource context. Structural checks cover direction, branching, partial data, cycles and filtering stability. Browser acceptance verifies both coordinate views, visible explanatory labels and legend, selection and navigation, and the owner-selected light/dark palette. A graph should explain its basic structure before the user opens an object card. @status:spec/plan
Shared Lens workspace, project coordinators, chat and history

org.vibevm.zap/lens owns one shared application server and platform-neutral client contracts. Quicklens is the browser/Electron presentation, Gamelens is the future game presentation, and Codlens includes the future VS Code and IntelliJ IDEA integrations as well as agent-facing integration assets. Multiple kinds of Lens may connect simultaneously. The separate org.vibevm.zap/zap engine remains authoritative for planning rules, economics, admission, plan versions and applied effects. The shared server coordinates services through public interfaces; it neither duplicates the planning engine nor depends on the host Vibevm source layout. @status:spec/plan

The shared server owns the project registry, project-scoped work contexts, coordinator and worker registries, execution control and dispatch queues, durable questions and answers, chat transcripts, event history, source watching and ZAP workflow composition. PROP-006 separates native child execution, optional managed terminals, product adapters and execution hosts. A renderer or an MCP connector does not instantiate a competing planning authority, workflow writer or source watcher for the same context. Thin local agent connectors and thin authenticated UI gateways call the shared application services. The existing durable broker and domain adapters are reused and consolidated rather than replaced solely to change presentation. @status:spec/plan

A project has a stable identity, display name and registered repository roots. Its work context identifies the exact checkout or worktree, branch/revision binding, planning store/campaign/base and coordinator conversation. Project, work context, actor, host session, conversation and client connection are distinct identities. A project has an explicit default work context; additional worktrees may have separate contexts. Every chat message, question, command and domain reference carries its exact project/context scope. Changing a client's selected project never changes another agent's working directory, context, authority or current plan. @status:spec/plan

Quicklens supports a focused project view and a board containing several selected projects. The board is a composition of separately scoped graph/read-model snapshots; it does not merge plans, invent cross-project dependencies or require a new global coordinator. Project identity remains visible on tasks, conversations, questions and history entries. Switching focus changes the user's view while other coordinators may continue. Cross-project commands or dependencies require an explicit supported operation rather than being inferred from visual proximity. @status:spec/plan

A user can begin development from a Lens client by selecting a registered project/context and starting a background coordinator through a configured host adapter. The lifecycle distinguishes starting, bootstrapping, ready, running, waiting for user, stopped and failed. The initial agent is explicitly instructed that it is the project coordinator, receives the exact working context, and follows that project's complete applicable boot contract; it is not launched under a worker quiet clause. The server records the session and bootstrap boundary. Reopening a client, switching projects or sending another message resumes the registered conversation rather than creating another expensive coordinator. Loss of resumable context or changed boot inputs is explicit; no guarantee of provider prompt-cache reuse or exactly-once model reading is implied. The default coordinator host and automatic-versus-explicit start policy are configurable owner preferences. @status:spec/plan

Each work context has one active coordinator binding by default, with many independently addressed workers or subagents. Independent contexts may run coordinators concurrently. Coordinator role is stated in the initial instruction and is separately enforced by scoped server capabilities; a model's role claim grants no authority. Delegated workers receive bounded task packets and their own actor identities according to the project's delegation rules. Workers may use the same question, message and artifact contracts without loading the coordinator's entire boot lane merely to communicate. PROP-006 separates task-appropriate, budget-aware coding profiles from inexpensive agents under test; concrete model/provider choices remain configurable. @status:spec/plan

Codex is the initial test product; Claude Code, OpenCode, Qwen Code and later products fit a capability-described adapter registry. A Lens-launched coordinator and a user-started coordinator are different launch origins, independently of whether their children use native or managed execution. Coordinator integration may use supported server/SDK/structured process protocols. User-started sessions may join through the existing broker integration while keeping their ordinary text workflow. PROP-006 defines native children and separately owned managed interactive terminals. Connection to an arbitrary already-open CLI or desktop session, concurrent input, idle wake and native resume are claimed only where the adapter supports them. Owned managed-terminal input is an explicit capability; unrelated terminal injection and transcript rewriting remain prohibited. @status:spec/plan

A Lens client provides a durable conversation with the selected project coordinator, with user messages, public assistant responses, execution summaries and linked questions or plan changes. The server persists user input before dispatch and correlates host thread, turn and public item identities with its own stable messages. While a turn is running, new input is visibly queued or steered through a supported host operation; ordinary send never silently interrupts work. Interruption is an explicit action. Unsupported delivery remains visible and retriable according to its actual state. Persisted, queued, host-accepted, running, answered, failed and uncertain are distinct observations. The server does not start model turns to poll for updates or to render history. Hidden model reasoning is not a promised chat or history artifact. @status:spec/plan

A versioned structured question request supports a group of independently identified questions, short headers, explanatory Markdown, optional per-question context and artifact references, required/optional answers, single choice, multiple choice, short or multiline free text, an additional custom answer with choices, option labels/descriptions/previews and nonbinding recommendations. Typed number, date, boolean, project-object and file/image-reference inputs can extend the same contract without changing the transport. Validation, draft answers, submission, explicit skip where permitted, cancellation, expiry, clarification, answer amendment and earlier answer versions have explicit meanings. A recommended or preselected option is not a submitted answer. Stable question and option identities survive client presentation changes. This common schema must represent ordinary native agent questions without forcing the user back to a terminal; host-specific unsupported fields remain explicit rather than being silently discarded. @status:spec/plan

The preferred agent-facing question action is ZapAskUserQuestion, displayed to the user as /ZapAskUserQuestion. Integration instructions supplied to coordinators and delegated workers direct ordinary user clarification questions through this action and require a short ordinary-text notice that the question was sent through /ZapAskUserQuestion. Concrete MCP tool naming or optional native slash-command aliases are host-adapter details, not a claim that every host has the same native command syntax. Publishing returns the durable question identity immediately. An agent may continue independent work; if progress requires an answer, its run becomes waiting for user without model polling. A reply resumes or steers the same addressed session through the adapter. Native user-question events may be mapped to this schema where interception is supported. Intrinsic host permission requests and exact ZAP Owner decisions retain their own authority and response contracts; a normal question answer cannot approve an unrelated action. @status:spec/plan

The shared server exposes a durable history independent of inbox completion: project/session lifecycle, public chat, question and answer changes, tool/execution lifecycle where observable, source-change signals, plan-rebuild requests, proposals, previews, holds, decisions, applied revisions and refusals. Every entry identifies its source, actor, project/context, occurrence and ingestion times, correlation/causation and source event identity where available. Native and ZAP events are ingested idempotently with durable cursors; original source ordering is retained. A server ingestion sequence orders the combined display without claiming a true global causal clock across independent projects. History coverage and gaps remain visible; events that were never captured are not fabricated. Credentials and hidden reasoning are not stored as ordinary history content. @status:spec/plan

Plan-rebuild history links the request and its human or source-change cause to the public rationale, previous and proposed plan identities, exact source basis, affected tasks/milestones, approval or refusal and the actual applied revision. A proposal, decision and applied product remain distinct events. Historical views use an immutable snapshot or an exact revision read from ZAP; absence of such a snapshot is explicit. Inspecting an old plan does not activate it. Restoring historical intent is a new proposal through normal plan admission, not a rewrite of the event log. The inbox is the pending-action projection of this shared history, not its sole storage or user interface. @status:spec/plan

All Lens clients use the same authoritative questions, chat, sessions and plans. Opening another client does not launch another coordinator or duplicate an answer delivery. Answer and command changes retain expected revisions and idempotency; multiple clients observe the committed winner and can explicitly amend where authorized. Current project selection, selected graph item, camera, presentation layout, theme and local drafts are client view state. Saved board definitions or user preferences may be synchronized explicitly without converting one window's focus into global project state. @status:spec/plan

Keep maximum behavioral reuse in server services and platform-neutral protocol/client libraries: validation, history and conversation state, dispatch, question semantics, agent lifecycle and plan workflows are shared. Reusable Qwik components provide chat, inbox, history and cards where a client can host them. Quicklens and IDE webviews may share these components; Gamelens may present the same semantics differently. Sigma/Graphology coordinates and game-world layout remain presentation concerns. VS Code and IDEA native extensions are thin host bridges for project/file/editor integration and connection setup; they do not reimplement workflow authority or the full server. Logical modules remain inside org.vibevm.zap/lens for now, with explicit import/build boundaries suitable for later extraction. @status:spec/plan

The local agent/API channel and the password-authenticated HTTPS web gateway remain separate as specified in PROP-003. Internet clients call only named, authorized application actions for registered projects and configured agent profiles. A chat or agent-start action is not an arbitrary executable, shell command, working-directory or proxy endpoint. Agent processes, host protocol endpoints, credentials and ZAP controls remain behind the local server boundary. Launch/interrupt/chat permissions are scoped independently of viewing and answering questions; new UI capability does not enlarge an agent or Owner credential. @status:spec/plan

The next prototype first establishes the common server/project/context boundary and rich interaction/history contracts, then the Codex coordinator and native-subagent baseline with a visible start-chat-question-answer-resume journey. Project switching and a combined board use the same services. PROP-006 then adds an optional local managed-terminal path before future mixed products, remote execution hosts and RLM strategies. Work preserves the paused prototype and known integration gaps without claiming them complete. Verification stays proportionate to the current architecture: meaningful checks of project isolation, actor routing, startup duplication and the demonstrated interaction path plus applicable required build checks; no comparative model pilot, exhaustive host matrix or prolonged cosmetic/edge-case refinement before further owner architecture input. @status:spec/plan

For a coordinator started by Wayfinder, the server assigns and retains its broker handle and records the correspondence to the owned coordinator session. A model-supplied native identifier does not establish that correspondence. A user answer first reaches the exact durable actor inbox; an answer-ready notice then uses the ordinary scoped dispatch queue. Busy sessions wait for a safe point, and paused or stopped projects retain the notice until Continue. A child answer may notify its known coordinator as a forwarding step with the original actor, question and answer version preserved; this does not claim child consumption. Unbound external agents retain their supported inbox delivery without a universal idle-wake claim. An owned Codex profile may explicitly preauthorize only named local question, context, inbox and acknowledgement tools, with delegation separately selected. This transport permission does not approve a plan effect, terminal command or native permission request, and it does not modify global host settings. @status:spec/plan

A local gateway establishes a separate scoped connection for each Lens client using a fresh short-lived pairing ticket consumed once. A reconnect or another client obtains another ticket from the same running Wayfinder rather than starting a second state owner or coordinator. The private bootstrap credential is not placed in a browser URL. A client disconnect releases its view and connection, not the project's work. Background refresh preserves the selected actor, question and draft within the same project/context; an older response cannot replace a newer focus. @status:spec/plan
Lens execution architecture: native subagents and managed terminals

The owner's development budget is a product constraint, with separate roles for implementation workers and agents under test. Coding workers are selected by task complexity, verification cost and available budget; the current Codex prototype may use inexpensive Luna for bounded work and stronger gpt-5.6-sol with high or xhigh effort when the coding task warrants it. Agents invoked to exercise product protocols or integration tests default to a low-cost capable model, currently Codex Luna, because those tests usually do not require a large coding model. Role-based selection survives a future provider change: concrete GLM, Claude or other model names belong to configurable profiles, not permanent protocol assumptions. Keep packets and live probes bounded, record the chosen profile and rationale, avoid redundant broad test/inference runs, and do not silently replace a cheap test model with a premium one. This instruction supersedes both the earlier universal Sol default and the subsequent universal Luna coding default; implementation-model choice is already authorized within the stated budget-aware policy. @status:spec/plan

Native subagents are children created and controlled through the coordinator's own agent harness. Managed agents are independent agent processes launched and supervised by Lens execution infrastructure, with real interactive virtual terminals that an authorized human can inspect and control. Role (coordinator or worker), launch origin (Lens or user), subagent ownership mode (native or managed), agent product/model, interaction transport and execution host are separately recorded dimensions whose valid combinations are capability-constrained. The initial managed mode requires a Lens-owned launch; merely joining a user-started session does not transfer process or terminal ownership. Starting a coordinator through Codex app-server does not turn its native children into managed agents. Earlier references to managed coordinators in PROP-005 research mean Lens-supervised coordinator sessions, not the managed-terminal mode defined here. @status:spec/plan

Project coordination, ordinary agent chat, ZapAskUserQuestion, history, plan control and the shared Lens clients must remain usable with native subagents and with managed execution disabled or absent. Native lifecycle and child controls reflect the actual harness capabilities; Lens does not invent a terminal or independently controllable process for a native child. Codex is the first implementation and test product. Other products remain registered adapter capabilities rather than assumptions embedded in the common model. Native-only deployment is a supported configuration, not a temporary stub dependent on managed-terminal code. @status:spec/plan

Enabled execution modes are the intersection of configured deployment policy, supported adapter capabilities, project scope and granted authority. A native-only profile does not advertise or dispatch managed launches. Unavailable modes or orchestration features return explicit unsupported or policy-denied results; no silent cross-mode or cross-provider fallback spends resources or circumvents the selected policy. This configuration supports changing product or licensing constraints without asserting that a particular provider currently permits or forbids a mode. Existing session continuity and a new run's mode selection are separate; changing a selector never converts an in-flight native child into a managed terminal. @status:spec/plan

The shared Lens server owns execution control: project/context registries, logical actors, tasks, run attempts, coordinator sessions, dispatch/admission queues, leases, budgets and durable execution history. An agent-host supervisor owns local processes and terminal handles and reports observed facts. A strategy proposes how to decompose, route and join work. ZAP remains the authority for the semantic plan, economics, holds and admitted plan changes. Execution scheduling does not become a second planning engine, and a process exit or strategy self-report does not establish task acceptance. @status:spec/plan

A logical task is distinct from a run attempt, agent actor, conversation/session and host process. Stable records bind project/context, task and parent task, run/attempt, actor, coordinator, product profile, execution mode, host, workspace binding and source/plan basis. Native thread/session IDs, process identifiers and terminal IDs remain adapter-owned correlation with explicit incarnation epochs. Multiple attempts may serve one task without overwriting earlier results. Parentage and project authority are validated independently of display names or process trees. @status:spec/plan

Delegated work uses a host-neutral packet containing the goal, selected context and artifact references, expected result contract, source/plan basis, available capabilities, resource limits, parent/depth and routing preferences. The coordinator follows the full applicable project boot and retains its long-lived session. Workers receive the context required for their packet rather than an automatic copy of the entire coordinator boot or every sibling transcript. Result artifacts, public summaries and acceptance evidence are distinct from console output. Concrete operating-system paths and protected environment construction are resolved by the selected host, not hardcoded in portable work packets. @status:spec/plan

A NativeSubagentBackend requests or observes coordinator-driven native delegation and maps supported harness lifecycle, messages and results into the common run model. A ManagedAgentBackend admits a registered launch profile through an AgentHost and creates an owned interactive terminal session for the worker. Both share actor addressing, questions, history, cancellation intent, result references and plan basis. Supported controls are capability-described rather than forced into an identical native API. The agent-product adapter, subagent mode and execution-host placement remain independently selectable. @status:spec/plan

Managed-terminal execution runs the actual interactive agent CLI/TUI in a real virtual terminal using the platform's supported pseudoterminal facility. It retains duplex input, terminal output, dimensions and lifecycle; an ordinary pipe containing headless JSON output is not represented as a live terminal. Structured agent events or APIs may supplement interaction where supported, while the terminal remains the actual session visible to the user. Terminal capabilities include inspect, subscribe, request input control, write, resize, interrupt and release control. The supervisor owns the registered agent process/tree; ending that agent does not leave an unrestricted shell as the next input target. @status:spec/plan

Many Lens clients may observe a managed terminal, but exactly one authorized controller owns its input lease at a time: the automation dispatcher or one human client. Acquiring human control fences previous automation input by epoch before accepting human bytes. Already running work continues unless an explicit interrupt is requested; input ownership is not the same as stopping execution. Human and automated input are attributed and ordered. Returning control is explicit, with the new context or intervention made available to the coordinator. Disconnect or uncertain partial delivery does not silently replay terminal bytes or resume competing automation. Terminal resize also has an authoritative owner so observers cannot fight over session dimensions. @status:spec/plan

The terminal view shows real observed output rather than reconstructed assistant messages. Terminal bytes, screen checkpoints, input attribution, dimensions and process/session epochs are distinct artifact streams with cursor and coverage information. Reconnecting a viewer resumes this stream where retained; it does not prove that a dead process or lost PTY can be revived. Structured chat, question, plan and execution events retain their own provenance. A terminal string that looks like a completion or approval is not by itself an authoritative ZAP event. Protected/raw capture and any redacted display are identified honestly; credential values are not ordinary public history payloads. @status:spec/plan

Execution control records a stable launch claim before provisioning or starting a process. The host registers run/session identity, owns the process tree, reports lifecycle and available usage, and accepts scoped interruption or cancellation requests. Requested, accepted, observed exit and judged completion remain separate states. Host/control-plane reconnect reconciles the existing run before another launch; missing contact means unknown status until resolved, not immediate success or safe duplication. Viewer lifetime is independent of process lifetime. Durable state and supervisor policy specify what survives server, supervisor or worker failure; Fractality's kill-on-supervisor-close behavior is evidence for one policy, not a universal reconnect guarantee. @status:spec/plan

Orchestration strategies consume scoped goals, context/result references, run state and budgets and propose work packets, dependency edges, routing, joins, local context processing or escalation. They cannot directly spawn processes, write terminal bytes, obtain credentials or bypass execution/ZAP admission. RLM-style recursive context decomposition and result aggregation is a future strategy above this seam; native delegation and ordinary managed fan-out can use simpler strategies. Context-by-reference, explicit sibling-result access, recursion budgets and aggregation contracts are architectural requirements; a learned router or full RLM implementation is not part of the initial MVP. @status:spec/plan

An AgentHost identifies the environment that executes a registered profile and resolves its workspace and artifacts. The MVP uses one local host. Future remote hosts implement the same scoped launch, observation, control and artifact contracts with independent host/session epochs; native local absolute paths or PIDs are not portable identifiers. Remote authentication, workspace provisioning, artifact transfer and scheduling are deferred implementations, not capabilities inferred from the presence of a hostId field. Product mixing and placement decisions belong to strategy/policy rather than Lens presentation code. @status:spec/plan

Quicklens, Gamelens and Codlens VS Code/IDEA integrations use the same execution services and actor/run graph. They may expose chat, inbox, history, agent tree and managed terminal in different layouts. Native children show their real available status, messages and results; managed workers additionally expose their terminal capability. Opening another client or board does not launch another actor, transfer input ownership or alter another window's project focus. Terminal rendering and native IDE integration are presentation/host bridges; execution authority remains on the shared server and AgentHost. @status:spec/plan

The localhost agent channel and authenticated HTTPS UI gateway remain separate. Managed-terminal observation and input are named, separately authorized capabilities scoped to an existing project, session, host and control epoch. Enabling chat or logging into Quicklens alone does not grant terminal input. The managed module may expose authorized terminal control through the UI gateway when configured; it never exposes an arbitrary shell/process/proxy endpoint or a raw host-agent listener. The rule against injecting input into unrelated user terminals remains. Sending bytes through an explicitly owned managed PTY is an intended, visible control operation. @status:spec/plan

Fractality is an architectural reference for mission control, per-run supervisors, work packets, journaled launch claims, resource limits, claim-check results and recovery. Its inspected prototype launches headless Claude Code with piped streams and one-shot stdin; it does not implement the managed interactive terminal required here. Study findings are recorded in LENS-EXECUTION-ARCHITECTURE-2026-09-15.md. Lens takes these boundaries as design input; it does not import the old Claude-specific launcher, retired provider subscription, historical research harness or entire Fractality product as a runtime dependency. @status:spec/plan

First revise common Lens contracts and shared-server ownership, then complete the Codex coordinator/native-child prototype with chat, rich questions, history and multiple project views. Next add an explicitly enabled local managed-terminal prototype demonstrating a real agent console, human observation, input-control transfer and ordinary completion reporting. Both modes must remain available according to configuration. Only later add mixed agent products, remote hosts and RLM strategy implementation. Verification is bounded to the demonstrated path and required project checks; no exhaustive host matrix, comparative pilot or unrelated edge-case refinement is authorized by this architecture update. @status:spec/plan
Project activity and agent operations workspace

The initial Quicklens workspace centers on selecting a project, viewing activity across all authorized projects or the selected project, inspecting the actual network of coordinators and subagents, and selecting an agent to see its available output and current work. These operations are the first product acceptance scenario. Chat, rich questions, plan views and optional terminal control are integrated into this workspace rather than made prerequisites for its usefulness. @status:spec/plan

A future unified canvas is distinct from the initial portfolio card page. It provides one pan/zoom coordinate space containing project regions and their task/milestone/agent projections. Scene references retain project/context/object identity, and explicit known cross-project relations may cross region boundaries. Selecting an object resolves its own project-scoped card or agent output. A shared camera or saved board layout is presentation state and does not merge agent contexts, plans or execution authority. Existing shared data contracts support this projection; a card grid is not claimed to implement the canvas. @status:spec/plan

Activity has explicit all-authorized-projects, project/context and selected-actor scopes, with filters for events requiring attention and retained history. Global activity preserves project labels and stable paged ingestion ordering with source provenance; it does not imply a shared plan or causal clock. A private/project view means scoped visibility, not a separately duplicated journal. Viewing or marking an event read does not acknowledge an agent's inbox delivery or answer a pending question. @status:spec/plan

The agent view represents coordinators, native subagents and managed workers with stable actor/session/attempt identities. Parent, delegation, communication or waiting relationships are shown only when sourced from the actual host or shared server. Agent names are labels, not routing identity. The agent network is distinct from the semantic task/goal graph, with explicit links between an execution actor and its assigned work where known. Selecting an agent preserves project scope and exposes its public output, lifecycle and available controls. @status:spec/plan

Output inspection shows captured public messages, tool/progress output and result references for the selected actor. Native actors expose only observed supported output and explicitly state unavailable or incomplete coverage; their display is not a fabricated terminal. Managed actors additionally expose their real terminal under PROP-006 control capabilities. Reading outputs or switching actors does not start a new model turn, reread the project boot or interrupt running work. @status:spec/plan

Lens makes Codex and other agent products useful as a coherent multi-project development system with VibeVM context, observable delegation and shared user interaction. The shared server supplies project/execution visibility and continuity while the configured agent products perform their actual work. Product-neutral contracts preserve this purpose when the selected agent changes. No claim about a competitor, future acquisition or provider policy is a technical requirement. @status:spec/plan
Zap branding and task model policy

Zap names the complete system. Zap Quick Lens is the external name of the current practical browser/Electron client; quicklens remains its internal code identifier. Zap Wayfinder names the central shared coordination/server component. Other Lens implementations are components of Zap rather than competing umbrella products. Existing package group org.vibevm.zap, module paths, CLI compatibility and protocol identifiers do not require mechanical renaming merely to change display branding. User-facing headers, titles, help and documentation use the agreed external names. @status:spec/plan

A versioned Zap model policy maps explicitly identified task classes and purposes to one of four model tiers plus an independent reasoning-effort request. Tiers are ultra, big, medium and small. Initial Codex bindings are ultra to gpt-6-astra, big to gpt-5.6-sol, medium to gpt-5.6-terra and small to gpt-5.6-luna. Bindings are configurable provider/model profiles; common planning and execution code does not infer tier, price or capability from a model name. Existing ZAP work type, role assessment and semantic routing remain distinct from these concrete execution preferences. @status:spec/plan

Rules select tasks by declared class/purpose and applicable execution scope rather than guessing from a display title. Implementation work and LLM actors invoked for product testing are separate purposes. Coding profiles are chosen according to complexity and budget; actual test actors default to a low-cost suitable profile. The selected rule, policy identity/revision, tier and concrete profile are retained with the execution selection. Ambiguous rules, missing bindings or disallowed profiles produce explicit resolution results, not a silent premium fallback. @status:spec/plan

Effort support is described for the concrete product, version, model, execution mode and invocation scope, distinguishing coordinator, native child and any relevant fresh/forked invocation: configurable with supported values, inherited from the parent, unsupported or unknown. Requested effort, resolved configuration and actual host observation are separate. An inherited effort records its parent/source and available effective value without pretending a child flag changed it; inheritance of effort does not imply inheritance of the model. A model match with an unreported effort does not confirm the full selection. Explicit unsupported values or unknown capabilities are not silently discarded. Default/inherit choices remain explicit. @status:spec/plan

Capability profiles and observed model/effort are trusted adapter evidence, not user-supplied authority. Provider-wide permanent assumptions are avoided. Current Claude Code documentation describes inherited effort by default and an optional subagent effort override; extended-thinking inheritance is a separate setting. This does not establish support in every installed version or invocation mode. A native-inherited profile remains valid where that mode is actually constrained. Codex is the only initial live test target; other-provider capability cases can be exercised as labelled fixtures. @status:spec/plan

Users can inspect and change authorized task rules and tier bindings through Zap Wayfinder and the shared client contracts. Changes use an expected policy revision and retain history. New policy revisions apply to future selections/attempts; running sessions retain their recorded selection and are not restarted merely because preferences changed. A per-task override is explicit and recorded. Public policy data contains model/profile references and capability information, never provider credentials. @status:spec/plan

Zap Quick Lens presents task class, model tier and effort as separate controls, showing the concrete resolved model. In inherited or unsupported modes, the effort control explains its actual source or unavailability instead of offering an ineffective selector. Agent/output views distinguish requested/resolved values from later host-observed values. The same data and behavior are available to other Zap clients through shared server services; the UI does not implement a separate resolver. @status:spec/plan

Focused deterministic tests cover four configurable tiers, task-rule selection, ambiguity/missing capability refusal, explicit effort, inherited effort without model inheritance, unavailable effort and preservation of an existing running selection. Policy persistence and UI integration are exercised through the shared application service. These are ordinary unit/integration tests, not a need to invoke large LLMs. The existing bounded-verification and account-independent checkpoint discipline remains in force. @status:spec/plan
Zap project pause, stop and continuation

Zap Wayfinder exposes separately authorized Pause, Stop and Continue actions for an exact project/work context. Project execution state is distinct from coordinator/worker process state and from semantic plan completion. Action requests, pending transitions and observed settled states have durable identities and revisions; all clients observe the committed project state. @status:spec/plan

Pause first prevents new dispatch for the project and retains its queued work and user input. It requests supported interruption or a safe stopping point for active owned coordinator/worker turns. The project remains pausing until the relevant observations establish that work has settled; unsupported or unknown control is explicit. No adapter claims to freeze an arbitrary in-flight LLM computation and later resume the same computation at the same token. Viewing activity, output and history remains available. @status:spec/plan

Stop prevents new execution, records cancellation/retention decisions for queued attempts and requests termination of the project's owned active work and resources. It preserves the plan, source/attempt basis, chat, question/answer history, outputs and available results. Process exit does not mean a task was accepted. Stop is not project deletion or repository rollback, and control of unrelated user-started processes is not inferred from an observed session identifier. @status:spec/plan

Continue restores the registered project context and resumable coordinator conversation. Before new planned mutations it checks current source/plan state and reconciles uncertain prior outcomes. Paused pending input is delivered through the same scoped dispatch mechanism; stopped/cancelled attempts may become new attempts with preserved lineage rather than blind command replay. A changed policy or UI focus does not itself recreate the expensive coordinator boot. Lost native context or unavailable resume is an explicit recovery state. @status:spec/plan

Pausing or stopping one project must not stop another project sharing the same model profile or account. Shared host processes are permitted only where verified project/session-scoped control provides this isolation. If only process-wide termination can enforce ownership, use separate project/context-owned host processes. Interruptions, process handles, descendant scope and incarnation epochs are validated before control; no generic kill-by-process-name operation implements a project action. @status:spec/plan

While paused or stopped, user messages, new specification signals and ordinary answers can be retained as input without silently restarting execution. An answer to a now-resolved native permission request does not authorize a later unrelated request. The UI distinguishes saved input, pending delivery and actual continuation. Explicit user Continue, with applicable scope and current policy, re-enables dispatch. @status:spec/plan

A bounded two-project proof verifies that pause/stop of A leaves B running and observable, repeat requests do not duplicate actions, retained history survives, and continuation reuses known session state without another bootstrap where supported. Deterministic host fixtures cover ownership and control semantics. The later owner request in PROP-012 additionally requires bounded actual lifecycle and background-delivery checks for all four priority providers using inexpensive models. Comparative model-quality benchmarking and destructive real-project tests remain outside this scope. @status:spec/plan
Zap product workflows beyond the transport MVP

A product workflow is accepted by its visible user outcome and authoritative state, not by the existence of a type, endpoint or transport demonstration. A generic shell in a PTY proves terminal behavior, not managed-agent orchestration. A provider hook proves only its observed integration, not a complete coordinator adapter. Portfolio cards are not a shared canvas. Existing accepted lower-level behavior remains the baseline while missing workflows are completed. @status:spec/plan

A local user can start Zap, open its browser or Electron client, add an existing project directory, choose an installed agent product/profile and explicitly start development without inventing protocol identifiers or copying synthetic multi-file JSON. The shared server validates registrations and owns durable configuration, project/context identities, provider availability and launch policy. The browser cannot submit arbitrary executable arguments or forge authority. Opening, focusing or reconnecting a client does not start inference. Advanced configuration remains available separately from the ordinary start flow. @status:spec/plan

Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode and Qwen Code are the current priority products. Registered drivers advertise observed version-specific structured conversation, native child, question, approval, interruption, resume and terminal capabilities independently. Common services do not assume Codex wire formats or universal provider controls. Installed, configured, authenticated, launchable and actually exercised states are distinct. Existing account configuration can be inherited through protected local launch configuration; credentials never enter browser payloads, prompts or ordinary history. Missing credentials are actionable setup state and never trigger a silent paid-provider fallback. @status:spec/plan

A provider need not expose a Codex-style turn identifier. Native identifiers retain their actual source and remain absent until observed or accepted by the provider's documented protocol. Zap-owned submission correlation is represented separately with explicit provenance and process/session scope. A successful send is not reported as rejected merely because a native turn ID is absent, and uncertainty after a side effect does not permit blind resubmission. Provider events and history are decoded against the actual installed protocol; local fixture shapes must not invent routes or identifiers. @status:spec/plan

All Zap-owned coordinator, provider-server and managed-agent launch paths support a shared outbound proxy policy with an optional protected profile override. Inherit, direct and explicit proxy modes have deterministic precedence over conflicting ambient proxy variables. Local Wayfinder, MCP and provider control channels bypass the external proxy, including localhost, IPv4 loopback and IPv6 loopback. Native child agents inherit the network policy of their parent process where the host supports inheritance. Credentials remain in protected server configuration and never appear in browser catalogs, task prompts or ordinary logs. TLS verification remains enabled. Applying the policy does not mutate global machine settings, alter already-running external applications, silently change providers or silently fall back to a direct connection. Unsupported provider-specific proxy controls remain explicit setup limitations. @status:spec/plan

Managed work is a durable task with a bounded packet, exact project/context and optional semantic work targets, parent/coordinator identity, model-policy selection, run attempt, actor and owned terminal. Wayfinder allocates identities and records a launch claim before spawn. The actual interactive agent CLI/TUI runs in an owned PTY; a structured headless stream is not relabeled as a terminal. Supported structured provider events and the authenticated Zap protocol supplement that real session. Reports, artifact references, process exit, cancellation and coordinator acceptance are separate facts. A human or authorized coordinator can create, inspect, interrupt and close work, obtain a worker report, and record its acceptance or required follow-up without polling model turns while waiting. @status:spec/plan

Every managed run receives a distinct server-provisioned broker identity and bounded task instructions for ZapAskUserQuestion, work transitions and result reporting. Its questions and results retain task/run/actor scope; human replies return to the same addressed run or an explicit retained/forwarded state. Multiple clients may observe, one controller owns input, human takeover fences automation, and control return is explicit. A terminal must be selectable from its real agent/work card. Closing a viewer preserves owned work. Restart preserves readable history and reports recoverable, stopped or unknown process state truthfully; it never blindly spawns a duplicate or replays terminal input. @status:spec/plan

ZapAskUserQuestion is a human interaction surface. A responder sees the project, requesting agent, relevant work/context, question purpose, options with descriptions, recommendations, requiredness, limits, deadline and whether other work can continue. It supports the ordinary rich question modes, custom answers, grouped completion, clear submission/delivery status, explicit cancellation and amendment history. Drafts survive the promised navigation/reload boundary without silently overwriting another client's draft or an already changed question revision. Keyboard navigation, labels, validation and status announcements are part of the flow. Existing artifact references are rendered safely or visibly unavailable. Native projection preserves only semantics actually supported by the provider; the richer Zap MCP protocol is not artificially reduced to one provider's native question shape. Ordinary answers never become permission approvals. @status:spec/plan

The unified multi-project canvas is now active implementation scope, superseding its earlier deferral in PROP-007. It provides one pan/zoom scene containing separately scoped project regions, semantic goals/cities/milestones/tasks/resources/routes and the relevant agent projection. Stable namespaced references determine selection and scoped cards; labels and screen positions are not identity. Layout communicates decomposition and known dependency order, with uncertainty and partial data visible. Project collapse, camera and selected objects are view state. No cross-project dependency or merged plan authority is inferred from visual proximity. Project switching, the common event queue, questions and terminal inspection remain available from the scene. @status:spec/plan

The main user flows use product language, useful empty/setup states, actionable errors and visible progress. Internal protocol names, raw identifiers, JSON envelopes and diagnostics belong in optional details unless needed to make a decision. Names remain Zap, Zap Wayfinder and Zap Quick Lens; internal quicklens, gamelens and codlens identifiers remain stable. Shared server/client contracts carry behavior needed by future Lens presentations. @status:spec/plan

Acceptance covers a real available managed agent receiving a bounded task, asking a human, receiving the answer and producing a report with explicit review, plus multiple projects on one canvas, provider-specific supported paths, setup/reconnect and the required package gates. Deterministic tests cover unavailable capabilities and authority boundaries. Actual model probes use inexpensive configured profiles and tiny isolated projects. No comparative model campaign, full RLM strategy, remote host system, real public tunnel deployment or native IDE shell is added implicitly. @status:spec/plan
Graph notes, deferred instructions and recoverable Trash

A human can attach a passive note or deferred instruction to a project, semantic object, relationship or work/agent reference. Its stable target contains project/context, reference domain and exact source reference; its recorded basis and object snapshot explain what the author saw. Note identity, author, versions, timestamps and history are durable shared-server data. Layout coordinates, labels and similarity are never routing identity. Passive notes do not dispatch agent input. Editing an instruction creates a new version rather than rewriting previously delivered content. @status:spec/plan

The default deferred trigger is before work begins on the exact bound task or milestone. Creating a note does not interrupt the active task, start a model, or silently change the plan. Managed launch and an explicit host-neutral begin-work protocol resolve known work targets and retrieve eligible instructions before work. Native work that has not declared a target remains visibly waiting for a matching work boundary; Zap does not guess the target from natural-language output. Queued, offered, read/acknowledged and explicitly resolved states remain distinct. Delivery is versioned and idempotent for the addressed work attempt, respecting pause, stop, authority and source changes. @status:spec/plan

The human can view, edit, archive or explicitly send a deferred instruction now. A note, ordinary reply or acknowledgement is not execution permission, Owner approval or proof of implementation. Agent feedback may explain that an instruction was considered, superseded or needs clarification, without erasing the original. Automatic suggestions of obsolescence remain distinguishable from a human archive action. @status:spec/plan

Trash is a recoverable shared collection scoped by project/context, with an authorized cross-project overview. It retains removed graph objects together with their notes and relevant source snapshot, relationships, former identity, plan/source basis, removal reason, actor and time. Individually archived or obsolete notes are retained too. Moving an item to Trash stops its deferred delivery. The current product has no irreversible deletion action for these records. Filters, collapsed regions, paginated/partial snapshots and temporarily unavailable data do not prove source deletion and cannot archive items. @status:spec/plan

An authoritative source removal or replacement preserves the old object and its attachments in Trash or an explicit unresolved-target state. Missing or changed targets are not silently relinked by matching names. The human can inspect the former context, restore an eligible note, or explicitly relink it to a current exact object. An unchanged stable identity can retain notes across new plan revisions while showing their recorded source basis. Delivery checks whether the current target and instruction version remain eligible. @status:spec/plan

Restoring a note is a versioned annotation operation with history and current-target validation. It does not replay an acknowledged instruction or restart completed work. Restoring an old semantic plan object is a proposal through the ordinary ZAP planning/admission path, not a write to a graph cache or resurrection of an old active plan. Restoring a visual board arrangement changes presentation only. These operations have different labels and outcomes in the UI. @status:spec/plan

The shared application service owns annotation versions, target resolution, delivery eligibility and Trash. Lens clients render the same scoped records and named commands. Coordinator/managed backend work transitions consume a shared future-work attachment port rather than a Quick Lens-only queue. Source observers archive only on sufficient authoritative evidence. Notes and Trash survive client disconnects, provider changes and ordinary account/session continuity. @status:spec/plan
Four-provider pause and background delivery

The same project lifecycle and addressed background delivery are implemented for all four registered provider families. Owned structured coordinators and owned interactive managed workers retain distinct execution mechanisms. Configured native integrations may report their actual supported session controls. Observing an arbitrary external session does not confer ownership of its desktop window or terminal. @status:spec/plan

Pause commits the project/context dispatch fence before requesting provider control. An already idle owned session can settle immediately. Active work is interrupted using a verified provider mechanism, and the project remains pausing until all relevant owned work is observed settled. An interruption request alone is not settlement. The same conversation, task lineage, questions, answers and queued inputs remain retained. Pause does not promise freezing and resuming a remote model computation at an identical token. @status:spec/plan

Explicit Continue re-enables dispatch for the exact project/context and resumes its known provider conversation where process recreation is necessary. It preserves pinned model/effort and trusted agent bindings and does not resend the full coordinator bootstrap. Stored source/plan changes remain available for reconciliation before new mutations. Stop is distinct from Pause; neither state can be cleared by a background event. A lost session requires an explicit recovery state rather than a silent new expensive coordinator. @status:spec/plan

An actionable addressed event creates a durable wake notice on the shared server. Notices retain project/context, intended actor, source event, question/answer version or child result identity, and delivery state. The server submits notice input through a verified provider route only when the exact owned session is ready and automation owns control. Busy sessions retain notices until an observed safe point; paused/stopped projects retain them until Continue. No model polling loop implements waiting. Multiple events may be coalesced without dropping their identities. @status:spec/plan

Persistence, claimed dispatch, host acceptance, observed reply and broker acknowledgement are separate facts. Retries preserve stable identities and fence process/session/control epochs. Uncertain transport after a possible side effect is retained for reconciliation instead of blind duplicate submission. A native turn identifier is stored only when the provider supplied it; otherwise an explicit transport correlation links the accepted message and observed response. Parent notification of a child result or reply does not claim that the child consumed an answer. @status:spec/plan

Managed workers remain real interactive CLI/TUI processes in owned pseudoterminals. Verified structured sidebands, provider server APIs or authenticated configured hooks may observe readiness and support control. Screen colors, prompt-looking text, quiet output and guessed delays are not authoritative idle or permission state. Human input ownership fences automated wake. A wake never answers a native permission prompt, grants plan authority or transfers terminal control. Interrupt and resume preserve the declared project and attempt. @status:spec/plan

User chat, rich question answers and amendments, meaningful cancellation notices and child-result availability use the same scoped dispatch discipline. Passive notes remain passive; deferred instructions stay attached until their declared work boundary. New specifications may signal changed source state without forcing an interruption of the current turn. Reconnect and restart preserve queued notices, their prior delivery observations and paused state. @status:spec/plan

Wayfinder owns lifecycle, queues and capability observations for every Lens client. Quick Lens displays requested pause, pausing, paused, continuation, queued wake and delivery failure distinctly. Controls are based on verified installed capabilities and current ownership. Opening another client does not create another wake dispatcher or duplicate a model turn. @status:spec/plan

Acceptance uses bounded actual checks for Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode and Qwen Code with explicitly selected inexpensive models, plus deterministic integration checks for project isolation, busy-to-idle delivery, pause retention, Continue, duplicate events, uncertain send and human terminal control. At least one actual idle agent must receive a late answer without having a blocking inbox wait in flight. Active pause is checked through provider settlement, and continuation reuses its conversation. Actual provider credentials, model availability or version limits are reported precisely; a fake process or a capability flag is not evidence of a real provider primitive. This is a support check, not a comparative model-quality benchmark. @status:spec/plan
ZapMockAgent and deterministic ZapMockModel

ZapMockModel is a deterministic algorithm, not an LLM wrapper. An explicit seed, scenario and ordered inputs determine its state, effects and trace. Time and gates are advanced explicitly by the test driver; model decisions do not depend on wall-clock timing, network randomness or credentials. Snapshot and restore preserve the same logical conversation and scenario position. Scenarios are a small validated test format, not arbitrary executable code or a claim to understand natural-language programming requests. @status:spec/plan

ZapMockAgent adapts that model to the same public agent, lifecycle and communication contracts used by real Zap integrations. It uses actual authenticated local HTTP/MCP, durable queues, question/answer acknowledgement, work reports and human review where the scenario requires them. It does not reach into application storage to manufacture success. A standalone process and an interactive terminal mode allow process/terminal supervision to be tested without a provider or model account. @status:spec/plan

The mock has its own explicit product and model identities and visible synthetic provenance. It is enabled deliberately in test/development profiles and is never selected as a silent substitute for a failed real provider. Mock success establishes Zap contract and orchestration behavior, not compatibility with a particular vendor CLI, authentication path or native protocol. @status:spec/plan

Initial scenarios cover a known response, a structured human question followed by an idle period, a late answer and explicit acknowledgement, controllable busy work, pause and continuation, checkpoint/restart, a managed result awaiting separate review, and two isolated actors or projects. Controlled failure cases cover duplicate events, stale epochs, uncertain acceptance and loss of a connection. Add future scenarios by composing the same small model actions rather than copying new ad hoc fake hosts. @status:spec/plan

Owner addition of 2026-09-16: keep reusable simulation scenarios beside the behavioral tests they explain. A scenario has a stable identifier, explicit feature coverage, deterministic seed and input tape, observable expected events and results, and its public-contract runner. Shared discovery validates and runs the corpus without an LLM. Support selecting scenarios and repeating them with recorded seeds; report the failing scenario, seed and input position so it can be replayed exactly. Separate pure model, local protocol, real process, real Git and provider-wire evidence; never describe a transport fixture as an actual provider test. A coverage index records supported features with scenarios and explicit gaps. New or changed orchestration behavior includes its scenario in the same change. Existing functionality is migrated into the corpus without pretending that undiscovered or missing scenarios passed. @status:spec/plan

Model actions remain deterministic data. The simulation harness performs bounded external effects through the product's real public contracts, inside isolated owned directories and local services. Process and Git completion are observed explicitly; logical scenario progress never depends on arbitrary sleeps. Actual asynchronous IO may use bounded timeouts to report a failure. Repetition creates fresh state and closes owned resources. The runner rejects unknown actions and unsafe file targets, and never evaluates scenario text as code or an arbitrary shell command. @status:spec/plan

Meaningful contract and product-flow checks run with ZapMockAgent first. Refactoring and interface mistakes must be detected before new live-model probes. After the mock gate passes, bounded inexpensive real-agent checks establish the provider-specific mechanisms that a mock cannot prove. Existing transport fixtures remain useful for native wire details; they are not relabeled as full product or live-provider evidence. @status:spec/plan

The mock requires no LLM API key, has no provider SDK or remote inference route, and does not inspect user credential stores. Its communication is restricted to the explicitly configured local Zap service. Test state stays in an isolated directory, owned processes and observers close naturally, and managed input obeys the same human-control lease, permission and project pause fences as production agents. @status:spec/plan
Repository workspaces, parallel plans and branch integration

A repository, a registered project, a plan context and a physical worktree have separate stable opaque identities. Git's canonical common directory identifies a repository binding on one execution host, not the repository's global identity. A project can be a subdirectory within that repository, and distinct projects can share the repository. Each plan context owns its conversation, coordinator, execution state, events and planning-service binding; it is not the planning algorithm's adopted-plan revision. Multiple contexts may belong to one project and repository. Existing default contexts retain their identities and checkout binding. Creating an independent plan prepares its owned worktree before any coordinator starts, preserving the project's relative directory within the repository. Algorithm-plan binding may initially be pending: preparing a working directory and starting the coordinator must remain possible before that coordinator creates or adopts an algorithm plan. @status:spec/plan
